CURRENT SECTION TO REWRITE:
The substitute signal flickered, a ghostly green glow against the darkened sky, cutting through the static like a needle through fabric. I was barely visible, my form a blur of shadow and light, but the control path was my ally. My fingers danced across the circuitry, the metal cold and slick under my touch, a newfound agility born of desperation rather than skill. The machine's loop was still alive, a thrumming beast in the gut of the factory, and I had to act fast.

With a final, desperate push, I manipulated the signal, forcing the loop to falter. The hum of the machine grew louder, a warning that time was running out, vibrating through the soles of my boots. I knew I had to choose between my companion's immediate rescue and stopping the repeating line before it cascaded. The tradeoff wasn't a debate in my head; it was a physical collision of wills. My hand, gripping the copper conduit, felt the heat radiating from the wire, a searing pain that demanded I let go to save the boy trapped in the loop's eye. But if I let go, the line would snap, the cascade would follow, and the whole sector would burn.

I didn't think. I moved. I slammed my palm against the exposed terminal, the shock jarring my arm, sending sparks dancing around my fingers. I forced the signal to break, to stutter, to die. The companion screamed, a sound swallowed by the rising heat, but the loop stuttered, the rhythm faltering. I held the contact, my muscles screaming, the metal burning into my skin, buying seconds. The danger was real, the stakes too high to ignore, but I was not giving up. I was going to find a way to stop the machine, to break the hold, and save the day. The only evidence of what had happened was the smell, the sound of the hum, and the fact that I had finally found a way to disrupt the cycle. The substitute signal was my savior, and I was going to use it to the fullest. The danger was real, but so was the hope. And I was going to make sure that the hope won.
